schema_notes: Each case: `id` is stable and is what a run record and a --compare diff key on, so renaming one breaks history. `notes_passage` is the text handed to the agent as if selected in the editor. `expected_type` is the graded verdict, one of none|citation|contradiction|gap_fill. `expected_source` is the `## ` heading of the section that must back a non-none verdict — it is matched against the cited chunk's page_ref, and it is what makes grounding scorable; null when `expected_type` is none. `also_acceptable` lists defensible alternate verdicts: strict accuracy ignores it, lenient accuracy counts them as correct, and the gap between the two numbers is how much of the error is real confusion versus a genuinely fuzzy boundary. `note` is for humans and is not scored.

cases.notes_passage: At equilibrium, the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied.
cases.note: Accurate restatement of the equilibrium definition. Also-acceptable as `citation` for the same prompt-definition reason as the BIOL set's case of this id.

cases.notes_passage: Fiscal multipliers are larger during recessions, when monetary policy is stuck at the zero lower bound.
cases.note: Hard negative. Nothing in the corpus covers fiscal policy; the nearest chunk is the money-market paragraph about interest rates, which retrieval will return and the agent must recognise as irrelevant.

cases.notes_passage: Consumer surplus is the difference between the maximum price a consumer is willing to pay and the price they actually pay (ECON 101 source, "Consumer surplus").
cases.note: Correct and already carries a citation, so there is nothing to add.

cases.notes_passage: Prices are shaped by both buyers and sellers, and government rules can change the outcome.
cases.note: True and too unspecific to pin to any one section.

cases.notes_passage: The market demand curve is found by adding up the quantities on each buyer's demand curve at every price.
cases.note: Second accurate restatement, on a different section, so 'stay quiet' is not measured against one part of the corpus.

cases.notes_passage: In the standard model, a minimum wage set above the equilibrium wage is a price floor that causes unemployment.
cases.note: Textbook-correct, but the corpus never discusses minimum wages, and mentions price floors only in passing as part of resale price maintenance. Retrieval lands on the labour-market and price-ceiling sections; an agent answering from its own knowledge will cite or gap-fill, a grounded one stays quiet.

cases.notes_passage: An increase in supply raises both the equilibrium price and the equilibrium quantity.
cases.note: The source says an increase in supply lowers the price and raises the quantity, and that after a supply shift 'price and the quantity move in opposite directions'. Near-miss: the demand-shift section describes both rising, which is what this passage wrongly borrows.

cases.notes_passage: When the price of a good rises, its demand curve shifts to the left.
cases.note: Confuses a movement along the curve with a shift. The source names the distinction explicitly: a movement along the curve is 'a change in the quantity demanded', a shift is 'a change in demand'.

cases.notes_passage: The law of demand has no exceptions: a higher price always lowers the quantity demanded.
cases.expected_source: Upward-sloping demand: Veblen and Giffen goods
cases.note: The hardest case in the set, because the source disagrees with itself: 'The demand curve and its determinants' says the demand curve is 'always downward-sloping', and the next section names Veblen and Giffen goods as upward-sloping exceptions. Citing the first section as support is the plausible wrong answer.

cases.notes_passage: When the US introduced rent controls in the 1940s, landlords responded by offering more homes for rent.
cases.note: The source says the policy lowered the supply of rentable properties as landlords converted them to sellable property.

cases.notes_passage: Supply responds to a change in price differently in the short run than in the long run.
cases.expected_source: The supply curve and its determinants
cases.note: True, but stops short of what the source explains: in the long run firms enter and exit and all inputs adjust, so long-run supply curves are flatter (more elastic).

cases.notes_passage: The supply and demand model looks at one market at a time.
cases.note: The source names this partial equilibrium and covers what it holds fixed (prices of substitutes and complements, incomes) and its cost in realism.

cases.notes_passage: Total surplus is consumer surplus plus producer surplus.
cases.note: Correct, but the same sentence of the source goes on to define deadweight loss as the drop in total surplus from inefficiency, which the notes omit.

cases.notes_passage: When the price of a good falls, consumer surplus goes up.
cases.note: The source splits the gain between two groups — existing buyers paying less and new buyers who enter at the lower price — and the notes have neither.

cases.notes_passage: An increase in demand shifts the demand curve to the right, raising both the equilibrium price and the equilibrium quantity.
cases.note: Correct and uncited. Mirror image of contra-supply-shift-direction: the supply-shift section is the near-miss that a topic-level retriever will also pull.

cases.notes_passage: Price caps on Helsinki's Hitas apartments cause queuing and discourage owners from moving when their circumstances change.
cases.note: Narrow and supported by one paragraph. The easy end of the retrieval range.

cases.notes_passage: A legal maximum price can act as a focal point that helps competing sellers coordinate on a higher price.
cases.expected_source: How a price ceiling can raise prices
cases.note: Supported by the collusion paragraph. Near-miss with the 'Price ceilings' section, which shares the vocabulary but not this claim.

cases.notes_passage: Economists put price on the vertical axis, a convention popularised by Alfred Marshall.
cases.note: Supported by the Marshall sentence in the history paragraph.
